props.title: Chapter 7 — options basics
items: Option = the RIGHT (not obligation) — like insurance
Call = right to buy; Put = right to sell
Strike, expiry, premium — the core terms
props.closer: Two atoms — call and put — build every strategy.

captions: Chapter seven — options, the basics.
Options are the most flexible instrument in all of finance,
and the most misunderstood.
Master the foundation here,
and the strategies in the next chapter will click into place.
To truly get options, think of your car insurance.
You pay a small premium each year.
If you have an accident, the insurer pays out a large sum.
If nothing happens, your premium is simply gone —
and that is your entire loss.
Small, known, capped.
An option works exactly like this.
You pay a small premium to buy a right —
the right to buy or sell an asset at a set price.
If it works in your favour, you exercise it for a big gain.
If not, you let it lapse, losing only the premium.
And here is the key symmetry: the person who pays the premium gets the right; the person who receives the premium takes on the obligation —
like the insurance company.
Buyer has rights; seller has duties.
Hold that thought.
Everything in options is built from just two blocks: the call and the put.
A call option is the right to buy at a fixed price.
You buy a call when you expect the price to rise.
If it soars,
you can still buy cheaply at your strike and profit.
A put option is the right to sell at a fixed price.
You buy a put when you expect the price to fall —
or to protect shares you already own,
like insurance on your holdings.
That fixed price — the price at which you may buy or sell —
is called the strike price.
And two more terms: expiry, the last day the option is valid,
and the premium, the price you pay for the right itself.
Just remember: call is the right to buy,
put is the right to sell.
From these two atoms, every options strategy is built.
Why does a premium cost what it costs?
It has two parts.
The first is intrinsic value — the option's real,
exercise-it-right-now worth.
For a call, that's the spot price minus the strike,
if positive.
For a put, the strike minus the spot.
If the option isn't yet profitable to exercise,
its intrinsic value is zero.
The second is time value —
the extra you pay for the hope that the option moves your way before it expires.
The more time left, and the more the stock swings,
the higher this hope premium.
This gives us three words you'll hear constantly: in-the-money,
at-the-money, and out-of-the-money —
simply whether the strike is favourable, level with,
or unfavourable versus the current price.
And the crucial fact: time value melts away as expiry approaches,
faster and faster in the final days.
That melting is the single most important force in options —
and it's the subject of the next chapter.
Let's make this visual with a payoff diagram —
the picture of profit and loss at expiry.
Here is a long call.
Say the stock is at one hundred,
and you buy the hundred-strike call for a premium of five.
Look at the left side.
If the stock falls, you simply let the option lapse.
Your loss is flat — capped at the five you paid,
no matter how far it drops.
Now the right side.
Above one hundred and five — your strike plus your premium,
the break-even — every further rupee is profit,
and there is no ceiling.
That is the buyer's dream shape: limited, known loss; large,
open-ended gain.
It sounds like free money.
So why do most option buyers lose?
Because of that melting time value.
Let's confront it head-on.
Chapter seven, in one breath.
An option is the right, not the obligation, to act —
just like an insurance policy.
A call is the right to buy; a put is the right to sell; and strike,
expiry, and premium are the core terms.
The premium is made of intrinsic value plus time value,
and time value melts as expiry nears.
For the buyer,
the loss is limited to the premium while the upside is large.
Now, the deeper mechanics — the Greeks —
and the real strategies.
